package_info.why_malicious: The default configuration enables the AJP/1.3 connector on port 8009, which is highly trusted and should not be exposed to untrusted clients. This allows attackers to send crafted AJP requests to read arbitrary files or potentially achieve remote code execution if file upload is possible.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Enables the AJP/1.3 protocol connector on port 8009, allowing Tomcat to accept AJP requests from any network source.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: AJP is a highly trusted protocol and should not be exposed to untrusted networks. The default configuration exposes this port without authentication or network restrictions.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal Tomcat deployments should restrict AJP to trusted internal networks or disable it if not needed. Exposing it to all interfaces is unsafe.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: AJP is legitimately used for integration with reverse proxies like Apache HTTPD (mod_jk), but only on trusted internal networks.
key_indicators: No requiredSecret or IP restriction configured

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: prepareRequest() method accepts arbitrary request attributes and fails to enforce requiredSecret for AJP connections.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Processes incoming AJP requests and allows arbitrary attributes, including those that can specify local file paths for inclusion, without enforcing authentication.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Accepting arbitrary attributes and not enforcing requiredSecret allows attackers to craft requests that can read arbitrary files or escalate to RCE.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: AJP connectors should enforce authentication (requiredSecret) and validate input attributes to prevent file inclusion.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: AJP attributes are used for legitimate request forwarding, but should be strictly validated.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Attacker sends crafted AJP request to port 8009 to read /WEB-INF/web.xml or /etc/passwd
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Allows remote attacker to read arbitrary files from the server by specifying file paths in AJP request attributes.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Remote file read via network protocol is a critical security violation.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: AJP should not allow arbitrary file reads from unauthenticated sources.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: None; file reads should only occur as part of normal web application processing.
key_indicators: AJP request with file path attribute

attack_chain.action: Tomcat starts with AJP connector enabled on port 8009, listening on all interfaces.
attack_chain.leads_to: AJP port is exposed to network

attack_chain.action: Attacker sends crafted AJP request to port 8009, specifying a local file path in request attributes.
attack_chain.leads_to: Tomcat processes the request and reads the specified file

attack_chain.action: Tomcat returns the contents of the specified file to the attacker over the AJP connection.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains access to sensitive files (e.g., web.xml, /etc/passwd, credentials)

attack_chain.action: If attacker can upload files (e.g., JSP) to the document root, they may achieve remote code execution.

behavioral_signatures: AJP requests containing suspicious attributes (e.g., file paths)
file_indicators: No requiredSecret attribute in AJP connector
network_indicators: Inbound connections to port 8009 from untrusted networks
AJP protocol traffic with file inclusion patterns
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Scan Tomcat server.xml for enabled AJP connectors without requiredSecret or IP restriction. Monitor network traffic for AJP requests from external sources, especially those containing file path attributes. Alert on any AJP traffic from untrusted networks or attempts to read sensitive files via AJP.
